evidence_passages.text:
**Short answer**

Browser-automation communities make directly conflicting claims. Some project READMEs say stealth patches *pass all public bot tests* or even *all bot mitigation systems*; other maintainers and adjacent projects say the same class of patches only helps against *simple* or *older* checks, and that modern detection still catches them. The publicly reproducible evidence I found supports the narrower claim much better than the broad one.

**What the communities claim**

- **Strong claim:** `puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth` says `puppeteer-extra with stealth passes all public bot tests`, and the same README says all `fpscanner`, `bot.sannysoft.com`, and `areyouheadless` tests were green in `v2.1.2`. It also provides a code sample that visits `https://bot.sannysoft.com`. Source: https://github.com/berstend/puppeteer-extra/blob/master/packages/puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth/readme.md

- **Strong claim:** `selenium-stealth` says it can `prevent almost all selenium detections` and that `selenium-stealth with stealth passes all public bot tests`; its example script opens `https://bot.sannysoft.com/`. Source: https://github.com/diprajpatra/selenium-stealth

- **Very strong claim:** `undetected-chromedriver` describes itself as an optimized Selenium Chromedriver patch that does not trigger anti-bot services like Distill, Imperva, DataDome, and Botprotect.io, and its repository “About” text says `Passes ALL bot mitigation systems (like Distil / Imperva / Datadadome / CloudFlare IUAM)`. Source: https://github.com/ultrafunkamsterdam/undetected-chromedriver

- **Qualified counter-claim from the same stealth lineage:** the `puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth` README also says there are still ways to detect headless Chromium and that it is “probably impossible to prevent all ways” to detect it. Source: https://github.com/berstend/puppeteer-extra/blob/master/packages/puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth/readme.md

- **Much weaker claim:** `playwright_stealth` says: “Don’t expect this to bypass anything but the simplest of bot detection methods” and calls itself a “proof-of-concept starting point.” Source: https://github.com/mattwmaster58/playwright_stealth/blob/main/README.md

- **Another weak claim from a community template:** `playwright-stealth-basic-ts` says its Playwright-plus-stealth setup `CAN be fingerprinted`, and `Will be detected by: Advanced fingerprinting sites, Cloudflare, modern anti-bot systems`. Source: https://github.com/railtools/playwright-stealth-basic-ts

- **Modern-patches counter-claim:** `rebrowser-bot-detector` says many public bot-test pages are 5+ years old, that some people wrongly think `puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth` alone is enough, and that modern detections include leaks such as `Runtime.enable`, source-URL leaks, main-world execution, Playwright init-script globals, and `navigator.webdriver`. Source: https://github.com/rebrowser/rebrowser-bot-detector

**Publicly reproducible observations that support those claims**

- **Supported fact:** old/public fingerprint-test pages do exist and are easy to reproduce. `bot.sannysoft.com` publicly reports checks such as `WebDriver (New)`, `WebDriver Advanced`, and `Chrome (New)`. Source: https://bot.sannysoft.com/

- **Supported fact:** `deviceandbrowserinfo` explicitly says its `Are you a bot?` page uses only fingerprinting signals and HTTP headers, and does **not** use IP reputation or user behavior. Source: https://deviceandbrowserinfo.com/are_you_a_bot

- **Supported fact:** `deviceandbrowserinfo` also has a separate interaction page that adds mouse movements, typing speed, form submission, `CDP mouse leak`, automation-framework stack traces, worker checks, and Playwright/CDP indicators. Source: https://deviceandbrowserinfo.com/are_you_a_bot_interactions

- **Inference:** because some public test pages are fingerprint-only by design, passing them can support the claim that a stealth patch hides **some static fingerprint signals**, but it does **not** by itself support the stronger claim that the patch prevents production bot detection generally. This inference is based on the test-scope statements at `deviceandbrowserinfo`. Sources: https://deviceandbrowserinfo.com/are_you_a_bot and https://deviceandbrowserinfo.com/are_you_a_bot_interactions

- **Supported fact:** Antoine Vastel’s 2023 article gives code and fingerprint dumps showing that new headless Chrome removed several older tells: the old fingerprint had empty `plugins`, `HeadlessChrome` in the UA, `hasChrome: false`, and `webDriver: true`, while the new-headless dump showed populated plugins and a much more normal-looking UA/fingerprint. Source: https://arh.antoinevastel.com/bot%20detection/2023/02/19/new-headless-chrome.html

- **Inference:** that article supports the narrower community claim that older public fingerprint tests became less discriminating once Chrome’s newer headless mode looked more like normal Chrome. Source: https://arh.antoinevastel.com/bot%20detection/2023/02/19/new-headless-chrome.html

**Publicly reproducible observations that contradict the broad claims**

- **Supported fact:** a public `puppeteer-extra` issue from January 10, 2024 says the README example itself was detected on `bot.sannysoft.com`, and the reporter also says `Cloudflare detects puppeteer too`; the issue includes the reproduction script and package versions. Source: https://github.com/berstend/puppeteer-extra/issues/867

- **Supported fact:** another public `puppeteer-extra` issue says Playwright plus the stealth plugin still allowed `bot.sannysoft.com` to detect the changed `webdriver`, and the issue includes reproduction code. Source: https://github.com/berstend/puppeteer-extra/issues/764

- **Supported fact:** a June 20, 2024 `puppeteer-extra` issue says `puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth` worked for `meet.google.com` with Puppeteer `22.1.0` / Chrome-for-Testing `121.0.6167.85`, but with Puppeteer `22.2.0` / Chrome-for-Testing `122.0.6261.57` Google Meet detected automation and blocked access; the issue includes steps to reproduce. Source: https://github.com/berstend/puppeteer-extra/issues/898

- **Supported fact:** another public `puppeteer-extra` issue says DataDome flags the CDP command `Runtime.enable`, and the issue includes a concrete code path and a proposed tweak. Source: https://github.com/berstend/puppeteer-extra/issues/788

- **Supported fact:** a 2019 `puppeteer-extra` issue reports that `bot.sannysoft.com` detected `Raspbian Chromium` through the user agent even with stealth mode. Source: https://github.com/berstend/puppeteer-extra/issues/119

- **Supported fact:** a public `undetected-chromedriver` issue from November 4, 2020 says the driver was detected by Cloudflare “Under Attack Mode” and got stuck on the “Checking your browser” page. Source: https://github.com/ultrafunkamsterdam/undetected-chromedriver/issues/46

- **Disagreement:** a public `undetected-chromedriver` discussion from August 2023 contains conflicting user reports: one user says the current version works on Cloudflare but not DataDome, another says Cloudflare still does not complete, and another says an infinite redirect means Cloudflare detected emulation. Source: https://github.com/ultrafunkamsterdam/undetected-chromedriver/discussions/1420

- **Supported fact:** `selenium-stealth` has a public issue from January 2021 saying the “new webdriver started failing.” Source: https://github.com/diprajpatra/selenium-stealth/issues/9

- **Supported fact:** the public `selenium-stealth` issues list currently includes reports titled `Browsers created with selenium-stealth do not pass pixelscan` and `godaddy login page detects selenium even with stealth`. Source: https://github.com/diprajpatra/selenium-stealth/issues

**What is actually supported**

- **Supported fact:** stealth patches clearly target well-known browser-side signals such as `navigator.webdriver`, `window.chrome` consistency, plugins, languages, WebGL values, and some automation globals. Sources: https://github.com/berstend/puppeteer-extra/blob/master/packages/puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth/readme.md and https://github.com/mattwmaster58/playwright_stealth/blob/main/README.md

- **Supported fact:** modern public test suites now check more than those classic signals, including CDP artifacts, worker-context inconsistencies, Playwright globals, and behavioral signals. Sources: https://deviceandbrowserinfo.com/are_you_a_bot_interactions and https://github.com/rebrowser/rebrowser-bot-detector

- **Inference:** the best-supported conclusion is that stealth patches can still help against **older or narrower fingerprint checks**, but public evidence contradicts the claim that they broadly “prevent bot detection” on modern defended sites. That inference is supported by the mismatch between README marketing claims and the reproducible issue reports above.

**Uncertainty and lack of good evidence**

- **Uncertainty:** many contradiction sources are GitHub issues and discussions, which are real public reports with repro steps, but they are not controlled benchmarks; IP reputation, hosting environment, browser version, headless/headful mode, and target-site changes can all matter. Sources showing those concrete version/environment dependencies: https://github.com/berstend/puppeteer-extra/issues/898 and https://github.com/ultrafunkamsterdam/undetected-chromedriver/discussions/1420

- **Lack of good evidence:** I did not find a neutral, controlled, versioned public benchmark showing one mainstream stealth patch consistently defeating current commercial bot detection across Cloudflare, DataDome, and similar systems under matched conditions. What I found publicly is mostly README self-claims, fingerprint-test pages, and user bug reports.

**Bottom line**

The conflict is real: some communities market stealth patches as if they broadly solve detection, while other maintainers and testers say they only patch a shrinking subset of detectable signals. Publicly reproducible evidence supports the narrower view far better: stealth patches can improve results on public fingerprint tests, especially older ones, but publicly documented failures on `bot.sannysoft.com`, Google Meet, DataDome-related checks, Cloudflare, Pixelscan, and site logins contradict the stronger “prevents bot detection” claim.
